title: Modular private connectivity and DNS resiliency notes
content:
Purpose:
A compact reference for a customer POC that needs a repeatable, modular private-connectivity topology plus DNS resiliency patterns. Focus is on: private ingress, controlled egress, deterministic DNS resolution across hybrid environments, and low-touch troubleshooting checks for on-site engineers.

Context / constraints (customer brief):
- Highly regulated customer: no direct internet egress from inference instances. All outbound must go via customer-managed egress/proxy stack.
- Hybrid: inference hosts in our Dedicated VPCs + some inference components on-prem (for data locality).
- DNS: customer insists on split-horizon resolution and internal-only records for model endpoints.
- Observability: need to capture DNS resolution paths, TLS/ALPN SNI, and per-request routes for audits.
- Typical cloud: AWS (Transit Gateway available), optional Azure landing zone in a later phase.

Goals for POC:
1) Prove private ingress where customer services can call Redwood inference endpoints without exposing public IPs.
2) Demonstrate a controlled egress path for all outbound traffic from inference instances through customer-approved inspection/proxy appliances.
3) Provide a resilient DNS chain so resolution works even during partial control-plane outages.
4) Produce a short checklist and automated tests engineers can run during handover.

High-level pattern (modular blocks):
- Control plane block (customer-managed): inbound Route53 Resolver endpoints (AWS) / conditional forwarders (on-prem) for split-horizon.
- Connectivity fabric: Transit Gateway (hub) connecting customer VPCs, Redwood Dedicated VPCs, and on-prem via VPN/Direct Connect.
- Egress block: dedicated Egress VPC with proxy cluster + Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) for inline inspection.
- Service exposure block: PrivateLink (interface endpoints) exposing inference APIs to customer VPCs, or NLB with VPC peering where PrivateLink is not feasible.

Why modular?
- Reuse blocks across customers and POCs: swap in different proxy stacks or different DNS resolvers without changing core routing.
- Clear security boundaries and least-privilege attachments (TGW attachments, interface endpoints).

DNS resolution chain (recommended):
1) Application DNS query (from inference instance) -> local OS resolver (systemd-resolved / dnsmasq).
2) Local resolver forwards conditional names (e.g., *.redwood-inference.internal) to a dedicated Resolver endpoint in the same VPC (Route53 outbound/inbound endpoints).
3) Resolver endpoint forwards to customer authoritative resolvers for customer-owned names (split-horizon).
4) If resolver endpoint is unavailable, fallback to an internal cached resolver (dnsmasq) that returns last-known-good IPs for a short TTL and emits an alert to SumoLogic/Datadog.

Key DNS patterns and rationale:
- Split-horizon: Use Route53 inbound endpoints + VPC conditional forwarders so customer private records resolve only inside their network.
- Conditional forwarding: Keep rules minimal: only forward customer zone(s) to on-prem resolvers; everything else resolves in cloud.
- TTL & caching: Set short TTL (30–120s) for model endpoints to enable rapid cutover, but cache on the resolver layer to avoid complete resolvability loss if control plane temporarily fails.
- Observability: enable query logging on the resolver endpoints and stream to central logging for audit.

Ingress strategies (choose based on customer preferences):
Option A - AWS PrivateLink (recommended):
- Redwood exposes inference service via an NLB + Proxy/termination in Dedicated VPC. We create a PrivateLink interface endpoint in the customer VPC.
- Pros: private connectivity, IAM policy controls, per-ENI security groups.
- Cons: cross-AZ ENI limits, additional ENI count to manage.

Option B - VPC Peering with NLB internal:
- Use peering for simple topologies. Attach NLB with internal IPs in Dedicated VPC and add peering routes.
- Pros: simpler for two-VPC setups.
- Cons: no transitive routing; not scalable for multi-VPC hubs.

Option C - API Gateway private + VPC link:
- Customer calls API Gateway private endpoint which forwards to a VPC link to our internal NLB. Good when we need API-level request transforms or WAF in front.

Ingress security knobs:
- mTLS at application layer for customer-authenticated calls.
- SNI-based routing where multiple customers share a front NLB.
- Security groups with narrow source CIDRs (peered VPC CIDRs or specific ENIs).

Egress patterns (customer requirement: inspection & logging):
Pattern 1 - Egress VPC + GWLB (recommended):
- All inference subnets route 0.0.0.0/0 to a TGW route that sends outbound to an Egress VPC attachment.
- Egress VPC has an autoscaled proxy fleet behind a GWLB that connects to customer inspection appliances or integrates with their proxy chain.
- Benefits: visibility, centralized TLS inspection, consistent policy application.

Pattern 2 - Private NAT + proxy chaining:
- Use NAT Gateways + managed proxies when GWLB not accepted. Less transparent for inline inspection but simpler.

Pattern 3 - Customer-managed egress only (on-prem):
- For strict customers, send outbound over DX/VPN to on-prem proxy cluster. Requires robust cross-site bandwidth planning.

Endpoint selection advice: interface endpoints vs gateway endpoints
- Use interface endpoints (PrivateLink) for service-to-service RPC (e.g., inference API). Good when you want per-customer IAM control.
- Use gateway endpoints for S3/Dynamo workloads to avoid per-request ENI overhead and keep large object transfer efficient.

Example CIDR and route examples (POC-friendly):
- Customer on-prem VPN -> TGW attachment
- TGW routes:
  - 10.10.0.0/16 (Customer-VPC-A) -> attach customer VPC A
  - 10.20.0.0/16 (Redwood-Dedicated) -> attach Dedicated VPC
  - 10.100.0.0/16 (Egress VPC) -> attach Egress VPC

Route table snippet for inference subnet (text):
- 10.20.1.0/24 -> local
- 0.0.0.0/0 -> tgw-attach-100 (egress via egress VPC)
- 10.10.0.0/16 -> tgw-attach-200 (peered customer VPC)

Operational checklist (POC validation):
- Connectivity:
  - ping/tcp connect from customer app to PrivateLink DNS name -> resolves to interface endpoint ENI IPs
  - curl with mTLS to inference endpoint -> 200 OK and correct customer header seen by Redwood service
- DNS:
  - Resolve customer-private name from inference instance -> hits customer resolver via conditional forwarder
  - Simulate resolver endpoint outage: verify cached resolver returns last-known records and alert triggers
- Egress:
  - Confirm outbound flows traverse GWLB proxy (check client IP logs at proxy).
  - Validate that direct internet access is blocked from inference subnet (deny default deny).
- Observability:
  - Query logs show resolver queries and responses with timestamps
  - Enforce VPC Flow Logs for inference subnets and verify traffic to egress VPC
- Failover testing:
  - Bring down one TGW attachment and validate that routing still reaches the egress/proxy via alternate attachment (if configured)

Troubleshooting playbook (quick):
1) If customer cannot reach PrivateLink endpoint: verify ENI SGs, endpoint acceptance (service consumer VPSA), and DNS resolves to eni.* IPs.
2) If DNS returns nothing: check resolver endpoint health, route 53 rules, and local dnsmasq cache.
3) If outbound blocked: check TGW route table and egress VPC ASG health; tail proxy logs for blocked connections.

Configuration snippets (POC reference):
- AWS Route53 forwarding rule example (pseudo):
  - zone: customer.local -> forwarders: [10.100.2.5 (on-prem-resolver)]
- Security group minimal example for interface endpoint: 
  - allow TCP 443 from 10.10.0.0/16 (customer VPC) -> eni SG

Open questions / tradeoffs to capture before final doc:
- Do we require per-customer dedicated PrivateLink services, or can multiple customers share a hostname behind SNI + mTLS?
- On TTL policy: how much operational friction does short TTL create for frequent control-plane changes?
- If on-prem is the single egress path, what bandwidth and failover expectations do they have?

Next steps (for this POC):
- Build Terraform modules for: TGW + attachments, PrivateLink service + acceptance workflow, Egress VPC + GWLB. (owner: Marco)
- Create a small test harness that runs the operational checklist automatically and reports pass/fail (owner: Ella).
- Schedule customer workshop: walkthrough DNS forwarding and failover simulation (owner: Aisha).

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep diagrams simple for customer slides: show 3 boxes (Customer VPC / TGW / Redwood Dedicated) with arrows and label "PrivateLink" and "Egress via GWLB".
- Record a 10-min demo of the failover test — very persuasive for compliance teams.

References / helpful links:
- internal confluence: SEC-Connectivity-1452 (resolver patterns)
- example infra PR: github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pulls/678 (baseline TGW modules)

End of notes.
